## TL;DR

Implemented `repoos servers --tailscale` to show locally registered servers alongside servers discovered on online Tailscale peers. Remote discovery uses `tailscale status --json`; if that command is unavailable or fails, the command falls back to the configured `remoteValidation` host pool. Each peer is queried over SSH with a four second timeout, and a failed query becomes an `unreachable` row while other peers continue. `--json` includes the host on each row. Combining `--prune` and `--tailscale` is refused before local registry reads, pruning, or remote calls, so pruning remains strictly local. The CLI help and user guide now document the option.

The requested scoped check passed, including a successful remote validation on the configured ThinkPad runner, local guards, build, UI smoke test, and user documentation build. The dedicated command tests passed as well.

## Work and rationale

The command previously mapped the local validated registry directly to a fixed JSON object and printed a local-only table. I kept local health validation and pruning in the existing server-registry module, and added a separate collection step for remote data. This keeps the local registry as the authoritative source for local rows while making the cross-host behavior independently testable.

The remote collector first attempts Tailscale status and parses the peer map, excluding the local machine and peers explicitly marked offline. It normalizes peer names from either `HostName` or `DNSName`, removing the tailnet suffix. If status cannot be obtained or parsed, it marks Tailscale unavailable and uses the configured remote host list parsed by the existing `resolveRemoteHosts` helper. On every selected host it runs `repoos servers --json` through SSH, not direct HTTP, because RepoOS servers may only bind to loopback. The process timeout and SSH connection timeout bound the time spent on a slow or offline peer. Remote failures are caught per peer and represented as rows with `unreachable` and a reason, so one peer cannot prevent the rest of the results from appearing.

Rows are collected concurrently. In text output, the host column appears for local, successful remote, and unreachable remote rows. The JSON result retains the local registry details and adds a `host` field; remote rows retain the data provided by their own CLI and have their host set by the local collector. Tailscale unavailability is separately exposed in JSON and explained in text output. The current implementation uses the configured `remoteValidation` host pool as the fallback source, consistent with the shared host parser already used by remote runner features.

I chose to refuse the combination of `--prune` and `--tailscale`. This is explicit to the user and has a stronger safety property than silently pruning only a subset: the function returns before local registry pruning, local listing, Tailscale status, or SSH commands. The test checks the refusal message and spies on both local registry functions to prove they were not called. No route or API was added, so CLI/API parity did not need changes.

The CLI help usage and description include `--tailscale`; `user-docs/cli.md` explains peer discovery, fallback, timeouts, unreachable output, host JSON, and the prune restriction. There is no new runtime dependency.

## Approaches tried

I first inspected the current `servers` command, the registry output model, the existing Tailscale utilities, and `remote-hosts.ts`. The server registry helper is purpose-built for local health validation and cleanup; the remote-host helper provides normalized configured peers and should not be duplicated. I therefore left registry internals untouched and created an injectable collector in the command module.

The collector accepts Tailscale status, configured hosts, and a remote execution function through options. That seam lets tests provide fake status JSON and fake SSH responses without requiring a real tailnet or SSH access. Tests cover peer parsing, a successful host beside a timed out host, configured-host fallback, and the combined prune guard. The standard executable implementation uses Node's existing child-process API, which adds no package dependency.

I ran the focused Vitest file first; all four tests passed. Then I ran `REPOOS_CHECK_CHANGED=main repoos check`. RepoOS checkpointed the current tree for remote validation, the ThinkPad runner built the tree and ran the changed-path suite, and the remote validation passed. Local format and lint passed, the project build passed, the UI smoke test passed, and the user documentation build and index checks passed. The generated `dist/` build artifacts remain untracked/ignored and are not part of the source change.

## Challenges and blockers

The Tailscale status command is best-effort: an installed CLI may still fail if the local daemon is stopped or unreachable. Treating both process errors and malformed status JSON as unavailable ensures the fallback path remains usable and produces an honest explanation. Peer status may omit `Online`; those entries are included unless explicitly false, matching the intent to avoid excluding peers when an older status payload omits that field.

SSH errors vary by client and platform. The implementation preserves the process error text for diagnosability and normalizes timeout messages to `timed out`. A per-host catch and `Promise.all` allow the overall listing to complete after individual failures. This session did not make claims about connectivity to real tailnet devices; remote behavior was exercised with injected fakes, while the standard check's independent remote validation used the project's runner infrastructure.

No blocking issues remain. The check emitted routine bundle-size warnings during Vite builds and one existing VitePress sidebar-link warning; neither caused a failed check.

## Key learnings

The project's remote host pool already normalizes shorthand, list, and rich row configuration, so CLI fallback can reuse that behavior without introducing another config parser. Also, the safe boundary for `--prune` is easiest to reason about when rejecting the option combination before any registry operation; a test can then prove the absence of both local deletion and remote execution. Finally, SSH is the correct probe transport for this feature because local loopback binding is common and should not be changed to make discovery work.
